USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Close a written Phase One text now and use the December 15 List 4B deadline as leverage, not as a unilateral gift or an automatic hike. Do not raise existing tariffs and do not roll back the 25% lists already in force; keep Huawei on the Entity List and off this tranche. In exchange for enforceable farm-purchase, IP, currency, and financial-services chapters, be prepared to cancel or further delay the Dec. 15 consumer-goods tariffs as part of a signed package—not as a concession in advance.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderately elevated, not existential. The United States still holds the main instruments of pressure—tariffs on roughly $360B of Chinese goods, the Dec. 15 threat on phones/laptops/toys, and the Huawei Entity List—and China has returned to talks and to U.S. farm buying after the Oct. 11 “Phase One” announcement. But the dispute is already biting U.S. interests: ISM manufacturing contracted for three months (September the weakest in a decade), Moody’s put job losses near 300,000 with more if escalation continues, IMF estimates ~0.6% U.S. output loss under current tariffs, and farm sales to China remain far below 2017 even after November soybean and pork bookings. A Dec. 15 hit on consumer goods would shift the burden onto households and retailers just as services have been the remaining cushion. That is why the score sits near +0.25 (between neutral and the +0.5 “material GDP drag / exposed export sector” anchor), not higher: labor and consumption have not broken, and Beijing is signaling it wants a deal. Action should stay near zero (negotiate). Escalating now would raise recession risk and likely blow up an unsigned but advanced text; a unilateral partial rollback would give away leverage while White House hawks and China still disagree on whether any existing tariffs come off, and while structural issues (subsidies, forced tech transfer) are explicitly deferred. The APEC signing venue is gone and the Nov. 16 Liu–Lighthizer–Mnuchin call was only “constructive,” so the job is to paper the deal, keep Dec. 15 as a dated threat, and refuse to empty the tariff arsenal before compliance is written and enforceable.
key_factors: Unsigned Oct. 11 Phase One (ag purchases, limited IP/currency/financial services; structural issues deferred)
Dec. 15 List 4B (~$156B consumer goods) still scheduled if no deal
U.S. manufacturing contraction and rising recession/job-loss estimates from existing tariffs
China demanding phased/proportional rollback of existing tariffs; Trump/Navarro deny any such commitment
Farm sales resumed (soy, pork) but still well below 2017; political pressure in farm states
Huawei remains on Entity List; TGL only extended 90 days and is not in Phase One
APEC Chile cancellation removed the planned Trump–Xi signing venue

sources_cited.excerpt: After Washington talks, Trump announces a "Phase One" deal in principle: China to buy roughly $40–50B of US agricultural products annually; IP and currency issues also cited. Planned mid-October tariff hike delayed.
USTR splits List 4: List 4A effective Sept 1; List 4B (including many cell phones, laptops, toys, apparel items) delayed to Dec 15.
List 4A takes effect at 15% (~$110–125B of Chinese imports). China's first tranche of the ~$75B retaliation also takes effect.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

China is pushing to drop the Sept. 1 15% tariffs on ~$125B and seeking relief from earlier 25% tariffs; Dec. 15 duties on ~$156B (phones, laptops, toys) widely expected to be scrapped if a deal is signed.
Trump said he has not agreed to roll back tariffs and would not eliminate all levies; White House split between rollback-for-deal moderates and hawks who want existing tariffs kept.
China said both sides agreed to cancel additional tariffs in phases; Navarro denied any agreement to remove existing tariffs as a Phase One condition.
U.S. factories contracted three straight months; September ISM worst in a decade; trade war cited as No. 1 recession risk; NY Fed 12-month recession probability 29%.
By mid-November Chinese soybean bookings were 8.0M tonnes vs 18.6M tonnes two years earlier; pork buying continued amid African swine fever.
Commerce extended the Huawei Temporary General License another 90 days (Nov. 18); Entity List designation remains.
Nov. 16 Liu He call with Lighthizer and Mnuchin: constructive discussion of core concerns; Kudlow said talks were getting close; remaining fights over IP/tech transfer and specified ag volumes.
Trump reiterated that scheduled 15% tariffs will be imposed on December 15 if a deal is not reached.
